Introduction

Put a year of them together and a picture forms.

Every policy we place and every advisor call we take tells us something about how companies are being built.

Key findings
Cyber became the most common line on new policies Vouch placed, overtaking general liability and property.
Solo founders made up a fast-growing share of applications.
"What do my customers require?" was the top question on advisor calls every quarter.
Questions about whether AI is covered entered the top five for the first time.

In 2026, that picture looked like this: startups bought more cyber and E&O coverage, more founders started companies on their own, and more of the insurance conversation was set by someone else, usually a customer.

This report pulls those threads together. It draws on Vouch's own policy, application and advisor call data from January through September 2026, set against what the broader market, venture and security data showed over the same period.

“
The common thread: insurance is increasingly something founders buy because a customer, a partner or a new kind of risk asks them to, not because a checklist says so.

1
Chapter One

Cyber and E&O climb the list

Cyber and E&O took a bigger share of what startups bought this year, while D&O took a smaller one. The shift says less about prices and more about what founders are worried about.

What we saw

Among new policies Vouch placed, the share that included cyber rose steadily from early 2025 through the third quarter of 2026. In the second quarter of 2026, cyber passed general liability and property to become the most common line on new policies.

Tech E&O followed a similar path, taking a steadily larger share of new policies over the same period.

D&O moved the other way, making up a smaller share of new policies by the end of the period.

What's driving it

Cyber demand grew without a price cut behind it. Cyber rates were roughly flat through 2026, with an average decrease of 3.3% in late 2025, and capacity remained steady. What changed was the threat: social engineering, AI-generated deepfakes and supply-chain attacks became the losses founders heard about. One supply-chain breach in 2025 reached more than 700 organizations.

E&O grew even as the market for it got harder. Copyright litigation against major AI developers and lawsuits involving AI chatbots made insurers more cautious, and some carriers pulled back from higher-risk AI products. More founders bought E&O anyway, often because their customers asked them to.

D&O remained widely available and competitively priced. The more likely factor is how venture money moved. Global venture funding reached $679 billion in the first three quarters of 2026, with AI companies taking 64% of the third quarter's total and roughly a third of it going to rounds of $1 billion or more. When capital concentrates in fewer, larger rounds, fewer startups reach the financing that usually prompts a first D&O policy.

“
Cyber demand grew without a price cut behind it.
2
Chapter Two

The rise of the one-person company

The number of solo founders applying for coverage grew sharply in 2026. It is the clearest change in who Vouch works with.

What we saw

Through 2025, companies with a single employee made up a steady share of applications. In 2026, that share climbed nearly every month, and monthly solo-founder applications rose well above the level of a year earlier.

Why it matters

A solo founder is usually a first-time insurance buyer with no finance team, no general counsel and no broker relationship. They need to understand what is required, what is optional and what can wait. That need shows up directly in the questions we heard on calls.

What's driving it

The same shift shows up across the startup ecosystem. Y Combinator says nearly one in five companies it works with now has a single founder, compared with 8.5% of its Summer 2016 batch. Carta's data shows more than a third of new U.S. startups are solo-founded, up 53% since 2019. Stripe Atlas reported that 63% of the C corporations formed on its platform in the second quarter of 2026 had one founder.

AI tools are a large part of the story. Sixty percent of Y Combinator's Spring 2026 company descriptions mentioned AI or agents. One person can now build, sell and support a product that once needed a team.

“
One person can now build, sell and support a product that once needed a team.
3
Chapter Three

What founders asked us

We grouped the concerns raised on Vouch advisor calls into the questions founders were asking, and ranked them each quarter.

The top question didn't change

"What do my customers or partners require?" ranked first in every quarter of 2026. Founders increasingly came to us with a requirement already in hand: a contract, a vendor questionnaire or a partner agreement that named the coverage they needed.

That tracks with how buyers are managing risk. According to Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, 48% of breaches involved a third party, a 60% increase from the prior year. When a vendor's weakness becomes a customer's breach, customers start writing insurance into their contracts.

"Which policies do I actually need?" moved up

This question rose from fourth in the first quarter to second by the second quarter, and held there. It came from first-time buyers and early-stage founders trying to separate what is required from what is optional. The rise in solo founders makes this question more common, not less.

AI entered the top five

"Is AI covered under my policies?" reached the top five for the first time in the third quarter.

The timing is not a coincidence. In January 2026, Verisk released new optional exclusions that let insurers remove generative AI exposures from general liability and products coverage. Combined with insurers' caution on AI-heavy tech E&O, founders have good reason to check whether their policies still respond to the way they use AI.

4
Chapter Four

When customers set the requirements

Customer requirements were the top question on our calls all year, so we looked closer at what was being asked for and who was asking.

What they're asking for

Cyber liability was the most common requirement, usually with a minimum limit attached. General liability, tech E&O and professional liability, umbrella or excess limits, and crime followed.

Who's asking

Enterprise customers asked most often, as part of vendor due diligence and procurement. Partners, platforms and banks came next, followed by security audits such as SOC 2, landlords, and healthcare systems vetting their vendors.

How the requirements show up
01
Limits above current coverage

The contract names a minimum limit for a specific policy, most often cyber, general liability or umbrella. Those minimums are higher than what the company carries today. They're usually written for much larger vendors, so a growing company often has to raise its limits partway through the policy term to qualify. That adds cost and takes time.

02
Deal pressure

The requirement surfaces late in a sale or partnership, typically when procurement asks for proof of coverage before signing. If a policy is missing or a limit is too low, the deal, launch or lease waits until coverage is in place. That puts the insurance timeline on the critical path for revenue.

03
Specific contract language

Beyond the policy and the limit, contracts often require particular terms: additional insured status, waiver of subrogation, and primary and non-contributory coverage. These control how the policy responds when something goes wrong and whose insurance pays first. The certificate of insurance has to reflect them exactly, or the customer can reject it.

“
Customer requirements were the top question on our calls all year.
Conclusion

What this means
for 2027.

The patterns in 2026 point in one direction. Founders are building leaner, selling to larger customers sooner and adopting AI faster than insurance policies were written for.

That changes when and why companies buy coverage. The trigger is less often a fundraise and more often a customer contract, a security audit or a new product feature.

For founders heading into 2027, a few habits will save time:

  • Ask for insurance requirements early in any enterprise sale, not at signing.
  • Know your current limits for cyber, general liability and E&O before a contract asks.
  • Review how your policies treat AI, especially if AI is part of what you sell.
  • Revisit coverage when your business changes, not just at renewal.

The companies that treat insurance as part of how they sell, not just how they protect themselves, will move faster in 2027.

Methodology

Policy data covers new-business policies Vouch placed from January 2025 through September 2026, excluding specialty products and broker-of-record transfers. Coverage shares reflect the percentage of new policies that included each line; a policy can include more than one line. Application data covers applications with reported headcount from July 2024 through September 2026; a solo founder is a company reporting one employee. Advisor call data reflects themes grouped from client concerns recorded on Vouch calls from January through September 2026. External figures are drawn from the sources listed below.

  2. Munich Re, Cyber Insurance: Risks and Trends 2026

  4. PitchBook, Q3 2026 Multistage Funds in Early-Stage VC
  5. Y Combinator, solo founder data (September 2026), as reported by Runtime Wire
  6. Carta and Stripe Atlas solo founder data, as reported by Solo Founders
  7. Verisk generative AI exclusions, as reported by Independent Insurance Agents & Brokers of America
